La COVID-19 et l’Alzheimer: un filet nég: COVID-19 and Alzheimer’s: A Neglected Safety Net
«Ma mère est dans sa chambre depuis mars: “My mother has been in her room since March. No one takes her outside to feel the wind or the sun. It’s like she’s in prison.”
Alors que s’amorce une enquête publique: As a public inquiry begins into the deaths that occurred in CHSLDs (long-term care homes) during the COVID-19 pandemic, an 80-year-old woman with Alzheimer’s has just been moved to a room comparable to “the hole” in prison, her family says. Micheline Baril has lived at the CHSLD Saint-Lambert-sur-le Golf, on the South Shore of Montréal in Montérégie, for five years. “You parked me here,” she still sometimes reproaches her husband. She has often thought of jumping from the second floor and has at times ripped off the window screen. “If you jump, you’ll hurt yourself and be in a wheelchair for the rest of your life,” her spouse, Paul Ménard, who could no longer care for her at home, warned her. Since March, Micheline’s life has taken another turn. After testing positive for COVID-19, she was put in isolation in Wing D of her CHSLD. The facility <l1>made headlines</l1> this spring for its staff shortage and its sharply rising number of COVID-19 cases. In June, Ms. Baril was placed in an empty room with no access to water (other than what came on her tray at mealtimes) and no toilet paper. “They moved her without telling my father. She had no change of clothes and no toiletries, like a comb or a hairbrush,” says her daughter Sylvie, outraged.
<strong>« Ma mère a été traitée comme un: “My mother was treated like an animal. With no phone and no television, she was crying and slowly dying.”
<strong>‍</strong>Les visites de son con: ‍Visits from her spouse were nonetheless maintained. The rules during the pandemic are rigid. Wearing a mask, a face shield and a hospital gown is mandatory, and bringing anything in from outside is forbidden. So Mr. Ménard secretly hid a case containing a tube of toothpaste and a toothbrush in his underwear for his wife. “My mother has been in her room since March. No one takes her outside to feel the wind or the sun. It’s like she’s in prison,” laments her daughter Sylvie Ménard.
Pour les personnes souffrant d’Alzheimer: For people with Alzheimer’s, conditions in CHSLDs have been particularly harsh, says the Fédération québécoise des Sociétés Alzheimer. Overnight, visits from caregivers and family members were cut off. “It created enormous anxiety, because these patients no longer recognized the faces of the people who came into the room. It disturbed them, and so they withdrew into themselves,” says Sylvie Grenier, executive director of the Fédération des Sociétés d’Alzheimer. The anxiety generated by this situation led some to stop eating.
«On a entendu toutes sortes d’histoires: “We heard all kinds of horror stories,” adds Ms. Grenier, who does not want to blame anyone. Some patients wanted to run away. As a result, many were given higher doses of medication.
«On a augmenté la médication afin que le: “Medication was increased so that people in CHSLDs would stay quiet. Many slept more. It was the only way,” Ms. Grenier explains. “Because to avoid medication, you have to keep them engaged, organize activities, look after them, take them out, get them walking…”
En l’absence de la famille et des proche: Without family and caregivers, all of that was impossible. In CHSLDs, patients were moved to a red or yellow zone. Often, relatives didn’t know where their mom or dad had been moved. Ms. Grenier spoke with several CHSLD directors. Some confided that they are not proud of themselves. “They were wartime measures,” she says, “in the face of a pandemic no one had foreseen.”
Cette réclusion, qui a duré environ un m: This confinement, which lasted about a month and a half, has left lasting effects on residents of Quebec’s CHSLDs, 80% of whom have cognitive impairments. This long isolation, Ms. Grenier believes, accelerated the progression of Alzheimer’s disease and increased confusion in many of them. That is what happened to Micheline Baril, according to her family. After her stay in “the hole,” she was more confused when she returned to her room, her spouse noticed. Dr. Judes Poirier, a researcher, professor and director at the Douglas research centre, agrees and explains that stimulation is vital for patients with this incurable disease.
«On sous-estime l’importance de l’intera: “We underestimate the importance of interaction with people. If we don’t make an effort to stay active and move, the disease will progress faster,” he observes. During the pandemic, walks in the hallways were banned for residents of CHSLDs and seniors’ centres. “For their own good, we deprived them of socialization, physical activity and memory stimulation. It was the worst thing to do. It’s like a deflated balloon. Once the air has escaped, you can’t put it back. It’s irrecoverable. That’s the problem.”
Du jour au lendemain, au pic de la COVID: Overnight, at the height of COVID-19, members of the Red Cross and the Canadian Armed Forces stepped in to help people with Alzheimer’s. Some had never been in contact with an older person. “When you work with them, you have to know how to understand and interpret their behaviour. That’s why we offer <l1>about ten video training sessions</l1>,” says Sylvie Grenier. The goal is to equip anyone working in a public or private care setting who has to support a person with a neurocognitive disorder such as Alzheimer’s disease. For the loved ones of people with the disease, these videos are a gold mine of information. They break down, among other things, the causes, symptoms, risk factors and stimulation strategies.
Quant à Paul Ménard, le conjoint de Mme: As for Paul Ménard, Ms. Baril’s spouse, he doesn’t want to make waves over her situation, for fear of reprisals. “I spoke to the director and the social worker at the centre and I gave them a chance to turn things around. I don’t want to blast them,” says Mr. Ménard, a former maintenance supervisor for power plants at Hydro-Québec. In the meantime, La Converse reached Judith Lecours, the director of nursing care at the CHSLD Saint-Lambert-sur-le Golf. We asked her whether it was normal that, when moved to a red zone, a patient ends up with no toiletries and no change of clothes.
«Cela se peut qu’il y ait des ratés quan: “There can be glitches when we’re rushing to transfer a patient who has tested positive for COVID-19. There’s no need to dramatize,” said Ms. Lecours, who notes that the situation is improving. “I have nothing to hide,” she adds. “We follow the ministry’s guidelines. Caregivers and visitors are still limited to one person at a time. We need strict rules so we don’t backslide on the number of cases.”
Enfin, le Dr Poirier rappelle que le Qué: Finally, Dr. Poirier points out that Quebec should expect an explosion in the number of Alzheimer’s cases. “By an advanced or severe stage of the disease, patients with Alzheimer’s don’t listen. They ignore staff and wander from room to room. In some places, units are sealed off with electronic doors.” “On top of that, medications have little effect,” he adds. “The only way to slow the progression of the disease remains cognitive stimulation, including social interaction, which keeps the brain active.” According to Dr. Poirier, governments have understood that, should there be a second wave of COVID-19, these vulnerable people will have to be taken care of first. “The authorities know that restricting family access is not the best idea in the world. Visitors will have to keep wearing a mask and a face shield, but that’s still 10 times better than seeing no one.” Dr. Poirier recently took part in a videoconference with experts from Italy, Denmark, Sweden and England. “They all came to the same conclusion: we forgot the elderly in CHSLDs to focus on hospitals. They dropped the ball on them the same way we did.
Il y a juste l’Allemagne qui a été un pe: Only Germany was spared a bit more.”
La raison? «Les Allemands ont mis en pla: The reason? “The Germans put strict protocols in place to avoid the risk of viruses spreading. A doctor working in a CHSLD can’t end up in a clinic where there are young children with measles, for example. That’s not the case here in Quebec.” Should there be a second wave, the authorities know how to manage the crisis and, above all, how to control it.
«On connaît maintenant les conséquences: “We now know the consequences for this vulnerable population that is people with Alzheimer’s. We are all more sensitive to their plight, and I hope the second wave will be smaller,” the researcher concludes.
